description_en: Tāpā Hiti East has three spouts, all of which face north. The one in the center is known as Taḥdhāḥ Hiti, and it is from here that the most water flows, the other two spouts are shaped as buffalo heads and often run dry. There is no record of the hiti's initial construction, however, a Viṣṇu statue on the eastern wall of the hiti can be dated to the 4th century. One could speculate that the hiti might date from around the same time. The hiti has undergone many restorations and alterations. The sourounding area was paved with bricks in 1685 and in 1996 the Lalitpur Sub-Metropolis and the Department of Archeology carried out some repair work. The monument has been poorly maintained and is now overgrown with weeds and filled with garbage. The historic stone pavement and most of the historic statues have been covered with cement mortar. The shrine of Sage Agastya has been damaged by rising damp and the lime plaster is peeling from its deteriorating walls. The water supply is extremely erratic; there is no water flow during the dry periods of the year. The spout usually dries up in December, with water returning as late as the onset of the monsoon season. Still, the central waterspout is a major water source for the community. Locals work together to clean the hiti once a year on the 6th day of the bright fortnight of Jyeṣṭha (Sithinakaḥ).According to a publication by the Lalitpur Municipality (The Stone Spouts of Lalitpur Sub-Metropolitan City2007, p. 24) the hiti's water source is located in Pharping. However, a legend claims the source to be Nyākhā Cuka. The legend further shows its connection to Hiraṇyavarṇa Mahāvihāra and Kwāḥ Bāhāḥ. According to the story, the principal deity of the Hiraṇyavarṇa Mahāvihāra was earlier located in Piṅgalā Vihāra of Kathmandu. During the reign of King Bhāṣkardeva Varmā, Kulāpāda Ācārya brought the deity from Kathmandu to Lalitpur and kept it in Nyākhācuka. Since there was no water to wash even his face when he was based in Nyākhācuka, he created a spout in penance. The hiti was therefore given the name Tapa Hiti and the word Tapa later changed into Tāpā (Local knowledge: Local resident, Śāhī, male, age 84).
description_ne: यस हितिमा तीनवटा उत्तराभिमुख टुटीहरू रहेका छन् । ती तीनवटा टुटीमध्ये बीचको टुटीलाई त:धा: हिति भनिन्छ । यस हितिको दायाँबायाँ राँगोको टाउको अंकित टुटी रहेका छन् । यी दुई टुटीबाट पानी प्रवाह नहुने भएकोले यिनीहरू प्रयोगविहीन अवस्थामा छन् । यो हितिको निर्माणबारे जानकारी दिने कुनै अभिलेख पाइँदैन तर हितिगा:को पूर्वपट्टि भित्तामा तेस्रो-चौथो शताब्दीको विष्णुमूर्ति स्थापना गरिएकाले हिति पनि लिच्छविकालमा नै स्थापना गरिएको अन्दाज गर्न सकिन्छ । नेसं ८०५ मा यो हिति परिसरमा इँटा छापिएको थियो । त्यस्तै विसं २०५२ मा ललितपुर उप-महानगरपालिका र पुरातत्त्व विभागद्वारा हितिको जीर्णोद्धार गरिएको थियो । अहिले यो हितिको अवस्था सन्तोषजनक छैन । निकासको राम्रो प्रबन्ध नहुँदा हितिगा:मा पानी जमेर पोखरी बन्ने गर्छ जसले गर्दा पानी थाप्नेहरूलाई धेरै असुविधा भइरहेको छ । पहिले बीचको त:धा: हितिबाट बाह्रै महिना पानी बगिरहन्थ्यो तर अहिले बढ्दो शहरीकरणले गर्दा जमीनमुनि पानीको सतह घट्दै गएकाले सुख्खा याममा धारा सुक्न थालेको छ, तर पनि वर्षा याममा पानी पर्न थालेपछि हितिबाट फेरि पानी झर्न थाल्दछ । वर्षको एकपल्ट ज्येष्ठ शुक्ल ६ (सिथिनख:) को दिनमा टोलवासीहरू मिलेर हिति सफा गर्छन् ।यो हितिको मुहान फर्पिङ्ग मानिएको छ (Lalitpur Sub-Metropolitan City, 2007, 24) । तर लोकोक्ति अनुसार यो हितिको मुहान न्याखाचुकमा रहेको छ । यो हितिको उत्पत्तिसँग सम्बन्धित कथाले यसको सम्बन्ध हिरण्यवर्ण महाविहार र क्वा: बाहा:सँग रहेको देखाउँछ । कथा अनुसार हिरण्यवर्ण महाविहारको क्वा:पा:द्य: पहिले काठमाडौंको पिंगला विहारमा रहेको थियो । राजा भाष्करदेव वर्माको पालामा कुलापाद आचार्यको नेतृत्वमा काठमाडौंको पिंगला विहारबाट क्वा:पा:द्य:लाई ललितपुरमा ल्याउँदा पहिले न्याखाचुकमा राखिएको थियो । न्याखाचुकमा राखिँदा मुख धुन पनि पानी नभएकोले क्वा:पा:द्य: आफैँले तपस्या गरेर ढुंगेधारा उत्पन्न गरेका थिए । तपस्याको बलले उत्पन्न भएको हिति हुनाले हितिको नाम तप हिति रहन गएको थियो । तप हितिलाई नै पछि तापा हिति भन्न थालिएको हो (Local knowledge: Local resident, Śāhī, male, age 84) ।

historical_events.event_name: Building of the Sage Agastya Shrine
historical_events.event_description: Śubharāja Mahājana established a shrine to Agastya above the central water spout.

This inscription is engraved on a brick located on the southwest edge of the Hiti. Although the inscription does not record an event, it can be assumed that it was intended to record the the hiti's paving with brick. The inscription doesn't record the name of a donor or craftsmen who might have carrfed out the work, however, it does state that Amātya Siddhirāma prepared the inscription with Harirāma, Nandurāma and Rāmeśvara Bhāro as witnesses.
The Lalitpur Sub-Metropolis and the Department of Archeology restored the hiti.
